detail.title: rein; horse-harness
detail.description: Pair of reins for horse. Composed of single plaited leather strap which divides into three plaited straps bound at intervals with light green-dyed leather. Further division into two separate bunches of three plaited leather straps which form the bridle and terminate in leather loops for attachment of bit. Immediately before loops, leather straps are bound together with light green-dyed leather. Front is covered with light green-dyed leather with applied red wool disks with spoke pattern in strips of blue, green and yellow cotton cloth, cut out sections, inserts of black cotton cloth and narrow bands of multicoloured dyed leather. Black cotton thread stitched in linear patterns. Smaller four triangular pieces are of similar composition but decorated on green dyed leather with cut outs filled with red wool cloth and black linear stitching.

detail.title: wall-hanging; marriage equipment
detail.description:
Wall hanging "Niger". Rectangular piece, composed of nine (9) hand-woven narrow cotton-threads strips hand-sewn together selvedge-to-selvedge. The decoration is organised in transverse bands with continuous weft-faced arrangement. Decorations are done in supplementary weft technique. There are 
- five white background bands with black design in form of two pairs of opposed triangles and bars
- four white background bands with red design in form of two pairs of opposed triangles and bars
- five black bands decorated with groups of four coloured lozenges (green, red, yellow, and white)
- two black bands decorated with the number "1991"
- three plain black bands: two at one end and one at the other end.

The strips end in loose warp threads.

Two abnormalities:
1. Two srips had been sewn the wrong way around, creating discontinuity in the weft-faced band.
2. In one strip a red design had been made instead of a black one, and a black design instead of a red one.

detail.title: textile; skirt
detail.description: Woman’s skirt composed of 22 narrow strips with two warp-faced patterns, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages; in addition there is a longer edging strip at the top of indigo-dyed cotton thread (with no patterning) which serves as a tie. All the thread is handspun. 19 of the strips have the same pattern, with a central band of magenta silk (alaari) thread flanked by two narrower bands of indigo-dyed cotto, and with two stripes of six threads of white cotton down the centre of the magenta band, while two threads of cotton separate the magenta from the indigo. The remaining 3 strips have a wide band of alaari silk and a narrow band of indigo, but no band of white cotton; these strips form a wide band of silk in the centre and another along the bottom edge, in such a way as to imitate a two-panel cloth of woman’s weave. The weft is of indigo, and the cloth has not been hemmed.

detail.title: gown; tobe
detail.description: Gown (rigai): oblong shaped body with very broad flared sleeves. Composed of 182 narrow strip plain woven lengths of light and dyed dark blue coloured cotton warps and wefts hand sewn together selvedge to selvedge. There is also evidence that a multicoloured narrow strip/strips were at some point sewn to the bottom of the gown: only tufts remain. The combination of warps and wefts is used to create a blue/grey tunic. There is a large long oblong pocket covering almost 50% of the front body panel.  The tunic is then decorated with extensive embroidery and cutwork using bleached white cotton. The patterns are geometric in shape and arrangement and can be found around the neck extending to a large spiral on the back of the tunic and covering the entire front pocket and across the chest. The tunic is hemmed around the neck and sleeves. Openwork.

Female hair band weaved with raw silk, excepting that of the blue stripe, made of of cotton. detail.description:
Cotton woven indigo dyed skirt. Made of seven (7) narrow strips hand-woven and hand-sewn together selvedge to selvedge. The central strip is narrower than the others. The ends of the strips are finished with a hem.

A strip of cotton cloth is stitched along the crest of the helmet and falls as a 120cm pendant, ending in a brown leather tassle with black and white plaited binding. The cotton strip is edged with black leather and white leather stitching. An appliqued white leather strip with diamond shaped cutouts runs centrally along the cloth, stitched with black cotton. The surface of the cotton cloth is very worn but shows evidence of woven threads and red wool. Two 14cm teardrop shaped pendants of similar design are attached with leather bindings to both sides of the helmet. Each pendant ends in lenghths of plaited brown leather joined together with leather bindings. Fixed to the top of the helmet is the remains of an animal tail [horse ?] encased in cotton with evidence of red wool.

The ends are simply carved in low relief with faces - eyes, ears, mouth/beaks, the eyes seperated by a tail-like form indicated with parallel incised lines. The rim edge on the sides is indicated with single incised lines, and the corners with vertical parallel lines in knife work, the corners themselves with short incised horizontal lines. The rim is inlaid with opercula, all present except for one piece missing at the point of a serious split, and one other. The dish shows traces of grease, dried out in some areas, with mould and detritus on the inside. The wood is probably alder.

Engraved on all four sides with scenes: a] left to right of walrus hunting: man and basking or surfacing walrus, massed walrus, man throwing harpoon from kayak at walrus; man about to throw harpoon from walrus, walrus with harpoon line and float attached, four kayaks with dead seal, or female walrus, last with harpooned walrus on its back; surfacing walrus, and three further kayaks and an unidentified boat. b] man firing an arrow at a goose, the goose alreday with an arrow [?] sticking out of its back; a canine looking at a kettle with a handle next to a harpoon stuck in the ground; an unfinished animal. c] two sod houses with figures, arrow pointing out of second house; series of sticks or harpoons stuck in ground; two further sode houses, the first with two people on top, second with a tethered dog on top, and a stretched skin [?]; three further sod structures; four umiaks stored on racks, the whaling harpoons above, and harpoon lines and toggles [?] dangling down. d] a caribou.
detail.production_ethnic_attribution: Made by: Inupiat Made by: Arctic Peoples

Amongst geometric patterning, outlined in brown, are crosses ('+') and confronted birds; most motifs have small hooks attached.  Worked in woollen yarns: tones of blue (indigo dyed?), brown (madder?) and yellow (weld?).

detail.title: print; bookplate
detail.description:
Newspaper clipping showing image of a carved Maori house lintel found swamp at Pukepoto, North Auckland. Published in The Auckland Weekly News. April 28, 1921. p.36.

Caption:
BELIEVED TO BE A RELIC OF PRE-MAORI DAYS: CARVED LINTEL OF A HOUSE FOUND IN THE SWAMP AT PURKEPOTO, NORTH AUCKLAND.
Evidence is accumulating that long before the advent of the Maori from Hawaiki there was a civilisation in New Zealand far in advance of anything that he (sic) found in the land. In our issue of April 21 is given an interesting account of the discovery of mile after mile of formed drains, evidently many centuries old at Pukepoto, in the great Awanui Swamp. Later, the unique ancient carving was unearthed at a depth of 5ft., while of the ancient drains was being excavated. It was found rsting in a bed of peat. The lintel is 8ft. in length and bears very little resemblance to any known Maori work. The find has aroused considerable interest, and offers many problems for discussio. The carvng is now the property of the Auckland Museum, where it is on view. A full account of its discovery was published in the second edition of the News last week, and is repeated on page 45 in the first edition of the present issue.

detail.title: figure
detail.description:
Description by C H Read in 1895:
Head probably of an idol carved in very soft wood and represented wearing a low crested helmet. The face is covered with brown kapa [barkcloth], but the nose is covered with a piece of some animal's skin to which some brown fur still adheres. The eyes are formed of pointed oval pieces of pearl-shell perforated in the centre: the left eye has a lump of tapa in the perforation. The open mouth is set irregularly with shark's teeth. The top of the helmet-crest is covered with twisted fibre cord, the strands of which are alternately brown and black. The cap of the helmet is represented by a broad binding of the same cord passing across the temples and down the back of the head. A band consisting of five strings of the same cord runs from the back of the head across the upper lip, and the neck is bound for some distance with the same, the lower part however being bare wood apparently in two pieces, one of which is cylindrical and perforated vertically. The sides of the helmet-crest were originally covered with the patches of the skin of some small animal (rat?) overlaid with dark brown kapa; but on the left side the kapa has entirely disappeared, while on the right side the lower three quarters are intact. The ends of the black and brown cord hang loose from the base of the helmet.

Registration slip description by C H Read written in or after 1895:
War-god consisting of a grotesque crested head with elongated neck, made of wicker-work of ie-ie & overlaid with a fine netting of olona-cord covered with red feathers. Cape (possibly a section of an ‘ahu’ula) made of red 'i'iwi and yellow mamo feathers (possibly some yellow ʻōʻō feathers) attached in bundles to an olonā fibre nae (net). The cape is shallowly curved and has a wide, almost straight, neckline and short collars.

On the proper right there is a piece of kapa (barkcloth) tied to the end of the cord. The plaited olonā cords also extend slightly below the collar where they are cut short.  
The edge of the nae is roughly cut in places, with the bottom edge of the nae extending past the feathers in some areas.

detail.title: cape
detail.description:
Cape (possibly a section of an ‘ahu’ula) made of red 'i'iwi feathers and yellow mamo and ʻōʻō feathers attached in bundles to an olonā fibre nae (net). The cape is curved but mostly flat at the bottom edge and has a wide, almost straight, neckline.  
The red 'i'iwi feathers make up the main colour of the cape. The yellow feathers are arranged into a small hoaka (crescent) at the centre top of the cape. Two curved niho (triangles) of yellow sit at the collar and narrow towards the centre of the cape where they connect. Some of the yellow feathers have been trimmed to give a crisp edge between the yellow and red sections. Alternating bundles of red and yellow feathers are arranged along the neckline. The colour of the feathers varies slightly across the cape; a square section on the centre left of the cape may have faded, possibly due to light exposure. The colour and shape of the yellow feathers varies across the cape, with some sections containing long fluffy and pale coloured feathers and other sections more vibrant and less fluffy feathers.  
The feathers are attached to a very fine olonā nae in bundles. The bottom edge of the nae has possibly been cut short and some remnants of feather bundles are visible along the edge. A plaited olonā fibre cord runs along the neckline and collars. The cords extend beyond the neckline, creating ties for fastening the cape. The plaited olonā cords also extend below the collar, where they are folded back on themselves to create loops.

detail.title: ornament (?); religious/ritual equipment (?)
detail.description:
Composite piece, made of a thick fibre cord (olonā) to which are attached five circular elements of basketry, made of the arial roots of the ʻieʻie plant (Freycinetia Arborea).
The basketry elements are circular in shape and brown in colour. Each is made with short pieces of ʻieʻie expanding from the centre, and connected with additional ʻieʻie pieces woven in a circular pattern. Four of the five discs show remains of small feather bundles, and seem to have been de-feathered. The feather bundles (possibly of 'ōʻō and iʻiwi), are secured with thin twisted fibre strings (possibly olonā and/or coconut). They do not cover the centre of each piece, nor do they expand to the very edge of the discs. The fifth disc is still partly feathered, and has a strand of yellow feathers (ʻōʻō) attached along the edge, and bundles of black feathers (ʻōʻō) in a circular pattern around the centre. Two of the five basketry elements are ornated with a pearl shell disc, kept in place at their centres with a peg carved of dark-brown/black wood.
The fibre cord connecting the basketry elements is plaited, and with a loop finishing each extremity. A short piece of twisted fibre string is loosely attached to one tip. The thick plaited cord is attached to the back of each basketry element with additional twisted fibre string (olonā), using two to five connecting points. One of the five elements (the feathered disc) is attached with a different mechanism: the thick plaited cord runs through the basketry work at the back, and is further secured at one other point with thin twisted fibre string.
